title: Fed Rate Hike Explained: What It Does to Your Loan
description:
What does a Federal Reserve interest rate change mean for you? The Fed raised its federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75%-4% on Sept 16, 2026, and held it there on Oct 28, 2026. Variable-rate loans and credit cards tend to follow (adjustable loans at their next reset): on a $300,000 loan over 30 years, going from 6% to 6.25% raises the monthly payment from about $1,799 to $1,847. Fixed-rate loans you already have don't change, and savings rates tend to rise, often slowly.

Sources: Federal Reserve FOMC statements of Sept 16, 2026 and Oct 28, 2026 (federalreserve.gov). The loan and savings figures are illustrative examples computed for this video, not offers or forecasts; the Fed's range may have changed since. Not financial advice.

scenes.say: One decision in Washington can change your loan payment. The Fed's target rate is now three and three quarters to four percent, after a quarter point rise in September.
That's the rate banks charge each other overnight. When it rises, banks' prime rate usually follows, and so do credit cards and variable rate loans.

Say you owe three hundred thousand dollars over thirty years at a variable rate. If it rises from six to six and a quarter percent at its next reset, you pay about forty-eight dollars fifty more a month.
A fixed rate loan you already have? No change.
Savers can win. If your bank passed on the full quarter point, ten thousand dollars in savings would earn twenty-five dollars more a year. Banks often pass it on slowly. And cuts work in reverse.
